newsitem.title: USA: Defense portrays McVeigh as "kid next door".
newsitem.headline: Defense portrays McVeigh as "kid next door".

text.p: Defence lawyers were attempting to save convicted Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh's life by portraying him as the "kid next door" who was deeply affected by the deaths of some cult members at Waco, Texas.

The same jury that found McVeigh guilty last week of blowing up the Alfred P. Murrah federal building, killing 168 people, Monday returns to the job of weighing whether he should be sentenced to death or life imprisonment for the worst mass murder in U.S. history.
The defence on Friday began its campaign to convince the panel that McVeigh should not die for the April 19, 1995, attack.

Calling on former neighbours and Army friends, the defence tried to counter the prosecution's image of McVeigh as a cold-blooded killer by showing that during his youth and early adulthood, he was just like millions of other Americans.
Defence attorney Richard Burr told jurors they would not be able to easily dismiss McVeigh as "a monster or a demon."
McVeigh, he said, was a person "who could be your son, who could be your brother, who could be your grandson, who loved his country ... who is just like any of us."

"They (the defence) have already done a good job to personalize, humanise Timothy McVeigh," Denver attorney and trial analyst Scott Robinson said. But, he added, the defence could not counteract the emotional testimony of bombing victims' relatives that the prosecution presented as it pushed for the death penalty.

Last week, the jury listened to more than two days of heart-wrenching testimony from survivors, victims' relatives and rescue workers who told of the horror of the bombing and how they have never recovered from the loss of loved ones or from mental or physical injuries. Many of the witnesses broke down in tears and several jurors also wept at times.

Some legal analysts said such gripping testimony made the defence lawyers' task virtually impossible. Public opinion was also against them. A Newsweek poll published on Saturday said 67 percent of Americans favoured the death penalty for McVeigh.

"If ever the death penalty should be imposed on an individual, it would be in this case ... and it is the collective judgment of Oklahoma," Oklahoma Gov. Frank Keating said on CBS-TV's' "Face the Nation" programme on Sunday.
Defence attorneys tried to bring to life for jurors the lanky young man with close-cropped hair who has sat expressionless before them during weeks of testimony.
Former Army colleagues described McVeigh, who served between 1988 and 1991, as a model soldier.

Defence witnesses brought out human details such as the bed sheets decorated with the comic-strip cat "Garfield" that McVeigh had when he was a young soldier, and that when he babysat for neighbours in his hometown of Pendleton, N.Y., as a youth, he ate them "out of house and home."

John McDermott, the McVeigh family's next-door neighbour in Pendleton from 1977 to 1984, said McVeigh was "always the kid next door." He broke down on the witness stand when he said: "I liked him very much, trusted him. I can't imagine him doing anything like this." McVeigh, too, reddened, showing more emotion that he had done throughout the trial.
The defence said a key part of its case would be McVeigh's reaction to the 1993 confrontation between federal agents and Branch Davidian cult members at Waco, Texas.

The prosecution maintains McVeigh blew up the federal building to avenge the deaths of about 80 Branch Davidians when their compound went up in flames on April 19, 1993, exactly two years before the Oklahoma bombing.
Burr said on Friday that the defence would explain to the jury why McVeigh "came to the conclusion ... that the government murdered people at Waco."

"The federal government, whom we rely on to protect us, to serve us, to be our servant, had turned the tables and ... had declared war on the American people," Burr said, describing McVeigh's beliefs.

Defence lawyers have declined to say whether McVeigh will testify. Some legal analysts have said his only hope of saving his life was to throw himself on the mercy of the jury, but there was no indication he planned to do so.
